capability: CRISPR guide design and off-target/site reporting — backend/routers/crispr.py (design_guides, score_guide), backend/crispr_offtarget.py (scan_off_targets), and gui/panels/crispr_panel.py, for all four Cas types the app offers (SpCas9, SpCas9-HF1, AsCas12a, LwaCas13a), on both strands, at full-length real scale.

failures.expected: Of the max_guides=10 guides shown for LwaCas13a on the 24,544 bp COL1A1 record — 24,523 candidates searched — at least one pair does not overlap, i.e. the panel offers more than one target window.
failures.actual: All 10 shown guides mutually overlap. Positions [10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 20, 23, 24]: ten 22-mers inside a 46-base stretch at the very 5' end of a 24.5 kb gene, span 14 nt. pUC19 is the same shape: positions [5, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20] out of 2665 candidates.
failures.why: This is the most user-visible failure of the round and it needs no external authority — the app's own status line says '10 guides shown (of 24,523 candidates)', which is false in the sense a user reads it. Root cause is mechanical and sits in three lines: for LwaCas13a every candidate's on_target_score is `round(0.5 + (0.1 if 40 <= gc <= 60 else 0.0), 3)` (crispr.py, Cas13 branch), so the score takes exactly two values; the sort key is `(-on_target_score, abs(gc_content - 50))`; and a 22-mer with 11 G/C has gc_content exactly 50.0, so the tie-break is 0.0 too. Every window with 50% GC is therefore fully tied, Python's sort is stable, and the surviving order is insertion order — ascending position. The user gets the first ten 50%-GC windows in the molecule, wherever the molecule happens to start. AsCas12a on the same record escapes only because its 490 candidates are sparser; its score is equally two-valued (0.6 / 0.4, verified over all 75 pUC19 candidates: 56 and 19).

failures.expected: A guide whose single off-target carries one mismatch at protospacer position 20 — the PAM-proximal seed, Hsu weight 0.583 — scores Sguide 70.6, per the pinned definition: hit score (1-0.583) * 1 * 1 * 100 = 41.7, aggregate 100/(100+41.7)*100.
failures.actual: specificity_score 50.0, the same value the position-1 case gives (that case passes only by coincidence).
failures.why: The GUI's off-target checkbox tooltip reads 'score guide specificity (MIT)' and backend/crispr_offtarget.py cites Hsu et al. 2013 and carries that paper's 20 weights verbatim (MIT_WEIGHTS compares equal to the pinned `hitScoreM`). But the weights are never applied to real data: `scan_off_targets` buckets hits by mismatch COUNT and then feeds `_mit_hit_score` the synthetic positions `list(range(1, n+1))`, documented as 'treat all hits in a bucket as the worst case'. Positions 1..n are the PAM-distal, zero-weight end, so t1 collapses to ~1.0 and a single-mismatch off-target is scored as though it were a perfect on-target match. The number the user reads is a function of the bucket counts alone. Position dependence is the entire content of the Hsu score; without it the citation and the weight table are decoration.

failures.expected: Two references differing only in where the guide's single 1-mismatch off-target sits — seed vs PAM-distal — yield different specificity_score.
failures.actual: Both yield exactly 50.0, from identical summaries {'0': 0, '1': 1, '2': 0, '3': 0}.
failures.why: The one-assertion form of the finding above, kept separate because it is the statement that survives any argument about which absolute value is right: whatever scale the app intends, a seed mismatch and a PAM-distal mismatch cannot be the same number under a score called MIT. A related orientation bug is latent in the same code and not separately testable while positions are ignored: `scan_off_targets` applies the SpCas9 weight vector unchanged for cas_family='cas12a', where the PAM is 5' of the protospacer, so index 19 is PAM-DISTAL for Cas12a — the exact reverse of the seed the array encodes. Fixing the bucket approximation without also flipping the Cas12a orientation would trade one wrong answer for another.

failures.expected: The SpCas9-HF1 response differs from the SpCas9 response in at least one field, for the same target with check_off_targets=True.
failures.actual: Field-for-field identical on both inputs: same total_candidates (326 / 5409), same ten guides, same positions, same on-target scores, same off-target summaries, same specificity scores ([100.0] on pUC19, [95.6, 97.7, 100.0] on COL1A1).
failures.why: SpCas9-HF1 is a selectable nuclease in the CRISPR panel's Cas-type combo and CAS_INFO describes it as 'NGG PAM · high fidelity · fewer off-targets'. In the router it is only ever `cas in (CasType.CAS9, CasType.CAS9_HF)`, and the off-target scan hardcodes cas_family='cas9' for both, so the option is a label over a computation that cannot distinguish them. The claim the panel makes is specifically about off-target counts, which is the one number the app does compute and reports unchanged. Either the specificity model needs a high-fidelity variant or the description has to stop promising one; shipping both is what makes this a defect rather than a missing feature.

failures.expected: For each of the 326 SpCas9 sites in full-length pUC19, the reported on_target_score is within 0.05 of Doench 2014 Rule Set 1 evaluated on that site's own real 30mer (4 nt 5' context + 20 nt protospacer + 3 nt PAM + 3 nt 3' context), per the pinned definition in gx/corpus/crispr/crisporEffScores-v3.1.py.
failures.actual: 317 of 326 sites disagree by more than 0.05. Worst: GACCTGCAGGCATGCAAGCT — Rule Set 1 0.004, app 0.690. The app's range over the 326 sites is 0.17..0.74; Rule Set 1's is 0.002..0.915.
failures.why: Adjudicated with the mitigation stated plainly: `_doench_rule_set1_score`'s own docstring says 'Real RS1 uses logistic regression; this is a simplified heuristic', so nothing here is concealed at the source level. It is still a defect, for two reasons. First, the name is the only thing that reaches anyone outside that file — the function is `_doench_rule_set1_score`, the field is `on_target_score`, and the GUI column is 'On-target' with no qualifier, so the disclaimer is visible exactly where it is least needed. Second, the mismatch is structural, not a matter of tuning: Rule Set 1 is defined on a 30mer and assigns weights to the PAM and both flanks (doenchParams positions 24 and above), while the app scores the 20 nt protospacer in isolation and has no access to the context at scoring time. No amount of reweighting makes a protospacer-only function reproduce it. The honest repairs are to compute the pinned model from the 30mer the router already has in hand, or to rename the score to what it is.

failures.expected: Spearman rho >= 0.8 between the reported on_target_score and pinned Rule Set 1 over the 326 real pUC19 SpCas9 sites.
failures.why: The consequence of the mislabel, quantified so the severity does not have to be argued. on_target_score is the primary sort key for `guides[:max_guides]`, so this correlation is the accuracy of the app's guide RANKING, not just of a displayed number. At rho 0.23 the ordering the user is shown is close to unrelated to the published model it is named after. Recorded as a distinct failure from the value mismatch because a fix that changed the scale but kept the same protospacer-only preferences would repair one and not the other.

failures.expected: At least 5 of the app's top 10 pUC19 SpCas9 guides are in Rule Set 1's top 10; the pinned Rule Set 1 best guide is GTAACAGGATTAGCAGAGCG at 0.9152.
failures.actual: 1 of 10 shared. The app ranks Rule Set 1's best guide 3rd, and the app's own best guide, TTACCAGTGGCTGCTGCCAG (app 0.74), sits at the 68th percentile of Rule Set 1 (0.233).
failures.why: The end-to-end statement of CR-8: this is literally the list of guides a user would order. Nine of the ten differ from what the cited model recommends. Kept separate from the rho test because top-10 overlap is what a user experiences and rho is what a reviewer can act on.

failures.expected: For each guide /crispr/design returns, its on_target_score equals what /crispr/score_guide returns for the same sequence.
failures.actual: 9 of 10 disagree, e.g. GGTGATGACGGTGAAAACCTCTG — design 0.6, score_guide 0.68. Every AsCas12a guide design returns scores 0.6 or 0.4 and nothing else.
failures.why: Two different functions write one field. The Cas12a branch computes `round(0.5 + (0.1 if 40 <= gc <= 70 else -0.1), 3)` inline; /crispr/score_guide runs `_doench_rule_set1_score` on whatever it is handed. The field is a single `GuideRNA.on_target_score`, coloured by one set of GUI thresholds (>=0.6 green, >=0.4 amber) and exported under one TSV column, so a green Cas12a row means only 'GC is between 40 and 70 per cent' while a green Cas9 row means something else entirely. The same two-valued number is also the max_guides sort key — see CR-10.

failures.actual: 10 of 10 disagree, e.g. CGTTTCGGTGATGACGGTGAAA — design 0.6, score_guide 0.7.
failures.why: Same root cause as the AsCas12a case, recorded separately because the Cas13 inline formula differs again (a 40-60% GC window rather than 40-70%), so there are three on-target scales behind one field, not two. It is also the sharper illustration: /crispr/score_guide will happily apply a Doench SpCas9 model to a 22 nt Cas13 crRNA, which is not a thing Rule Set 1 is defined for either.

failures.expected: /crispr/score_guide refuses a legal-length guide containing a non-nucleotide character with HTTP 4xx, the way /crispr/design refuses the same alphabet in a target (companion test test_cr_13_design_refuses_a_non_dna_target passes for all four).
failures.actual: HTTP 200 with a confident verdict in every case: 'ACGTACGTACGTACGTACG!' -> recommendation 'Good', on_target_score 0.6, gc_content 50.0; 'ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGU' -> 'Good', 0.6, 50.0; 'ACGTACGTACGT12ACGTAC' -> 'Good', 0.6, 45.0; a tab -> 'Good', 0.62, 50.0.
failures.why: Directly the family #87 closed for the primer endpoints: one capability, two endpoints, one verdict on an input that is not a sequence. /crispr/score_guide validates length (17..24) and nothing else, then computes GC over the raw string — so '!' and a tab are silently counted as non-G/C bases and the percentage is arithmetically wrong as well as meaningless. The 'U' case is the one most likely to reach a real user: pasting an RNA-written crRNA into a guide-scoring box is an ordinary mistake, and the app answers 'Good' instead of saying the input is RNA. A 4xx here costs one `if` and matches what the sibling endpoint already does.

failures.expected: On a circular molecule the candidate count includes sites that run through the origin: pUC19 330 SpCas9 / 76 AsCas12a, NC_001699.1 543 / 257, AF071878.1 325 / 62.
failures.actual: The linear counts in every case: pUC19 326 / 75, NC_001699.1 541 / 256, AF071878.1 320 / 62 — 4, 2 and 5 SpCas9 sites and 1, 1 and 0 AsCas12a sites missing. (The AF071878.1 AsCas12a case passes: its origin junction happens to carry no TTTV site, which is why three molecules are pinned rather than one.)
failures.why: Ranked last of this round's findings and qualified, because unlike the others this is a capability gap rather than wrong arithmetic: CRISPRDesignRequest has no is_circular field, so the router is not ignoring information it was given. It is still the app's defect and not the caller's. The app's own Sequence model carries is_circular, the restriction capability already honours it (gx round 1, RE-5/RE-6), and gui/panels/crispr_panel.py:set_target is handed the loaded record's sequence with the circularity dropped on the floor — so designing guides against a plasmid, which is the single most common thing a desktop cloning tool is pointed at, silently cannot see the junction. The counts are small in absolute terms; the reason to record them is that the user is given no signal that a region of their molecule was never searched. Fixing it is the same doubled-sequence trick backend/routers/primers.py already uses.

notes:
Command: `PYTHONPATH=. backend/.venv/bin/python -m pytest gx/crispr/ -q -p no:cacheprovider`. In-process and offline — the tests import backend.routers.crispr directly, the way gui/panels/crispr_panel.py:_run_design does, and read every input from gx/corpus/inputs/. `ruff check gx/crispr/` is clean. Nothing under backend/ or gui/ was touched; version.py was not bumped and no tag was pushed.

Scope note: the commit was rebased onto origin/main ffd6e7f (another party landed the coords fix #94 and the 0.6.1 bump mid-round). The suite was re-run after the rebase with the identical 20-failed/150-passed result, and that is the run recorded here.

CORPUS LICENCE, flagged rather than decided: the two pinned CRISPOR files are the only way found to byte-pin the two published scores this app names, but their licence is contested by the upstream author's own files. The LICENSE.txt at the v3.1 tag is CC BY-NC 3.0; the LICENSE.txt at master states 'Up to and including version 3.1, the source code files crisporEffScores.py and crispor.py were licensed under GPLv3'. Both texts are pinned beside the sources and the conflict is written out in MANIFEST.json. v3.1 was chosen precisely because master's current terms restrict later versions to academic use. Neither file is imported by anything: the numeric tables are re-typed into gx/crispr/crispr_oracle.py, which asserts each one against the pinned bytes at import time, so deleting both .py files leaves a working oracle and loses only the byte-level pin. Worth a human decision before this sits in a public MIT repository advertising itself as free and open.

UNVERIFIED, deliberately: CR-4's literature half. The primary sources for the 5' placement of the Cas12a PAM (Zetsche et al. 2015, PMID 26422227 — 'the PAM for FnCpf1 is located upstream of the 5' end of the displaced strand of the protospacer and has the sequence 5'-TTN') and for LwaCas13a having no protospacer flanking site (Abudayyeh et al. 2017, PMID 28976959 — 'no significant PFS motif for LwaCas13a') are PMC author manuscripts whose permissions grant text mining and fair use only, not redistribution. They are cited by PMID and their bytes are NOT pinned. The SpCas9 NGG half IS byte-pinned, via CRISPOR's PAM table. What CR-4 therefore tests is self-consistency — the PAM read out of the raw sequence by index must match the grammar the app itself reports — and that passed for all four Cas types on all four inputs.

A second thing deliberately NOT filed: the app searches TTTV for AsCas12a where Zetsche reports TTTN. TTTV is a widely used design convention (it avoids a poly-T Pol III terminator) and CRISPOR's own PAM menu lists 'TTTV ... recommended, 23bp guides' against 'TTTN ... low efficiency'. The app is self-consistent and follows the convention, so it is held to its own TTTV claim. Recorded here so a later round does not mistake it for an oversight.

What PASSED, and is therefore now evidence rather than assumption — this is the half of the round that matters most, because the three prior-art defects are the ones a regression would bring back:
  * CR-1: total_candidates equals an independent both-strand regex scan, exactly, for all 4 Cas types on all 4 inputs (16 cases). pUC19 326/326/75/2665, NC_001699.1 541/541/256/5109, AF071878.1 320/320/62/1972, COL1A1 5409/5409/490/24523. The Cas13 last window (#64.1) is present; the Cas12a minus strand (#64.2) is present.
  * CR-2/CR-3/CR-4/CR-5: every guide the app returns across those 16 cases re-extracts by index — protospacer equals target[p:p+L] (or Biopython's reverse complement of it on the minus strand), the PAM is disjoint from the guide footprint, guide+PAM is a contiguous real stretch of the molecule, and the PAM matches its grammar. #53's off-by-one, where the PAM's N was captured as the guide's last base and the error landed in the PAM-proximal seed, is gone and stays gone on both strands.
  * CR-6: guide_length honoured for every length 17..24 on every Cas type, with total_candidates moving to match, on pUC19 and again at 24.5 kb (#64.3).
  * CR-7: every reported gc_content equals Biopython's gc_fraction of the reported sequence, to the decimal.

Pattern across the seven defects: the index arithmetic — the thing #53 and #64 were about, and the thing a guide designer most obviously has to get right — is now correct everywhere I could reach it. What is wrong is everything built on top of the indices. Three of the four numbers in the results table (on-target, off-targets, specificity) are either a two-valued GC flag, a citation with the cited computation removed, or the same value for a nuclease the panel promises is different; and the ranking those numbers drive decides which ten of 24,523 candidates the user ever sees. CR-10 is where that compounds into something a user would call broken.

Round 2 leads, not pursued here: (a) /crispr/design accepts N in the target alphabet and will return guides containing N — no pinned input has an assembly gap, so this went untested rather than unverified; a real N-bearing contig would settle it. (b) The reported `pam` field is the motif literal ('NGG') and never the instance ('AGG'), so the panel's PAM column is a constant; CR-4 deliberately tests the weaker grammar reading, and whether the instance should be reported is a product question. (c) off_target_count and specificity are computed only against [target] + reference_sequences, which the docstring is honest about, but the GUI exposes no way to supply reference_sequences — so every specificity number a GUI user sees is scoped to the pasted sequence alone.
